_spec.purpose: A standalone web edition of the archived visual story.
_spec.law: Facts resolve to the original verified claim record. A layout rebuild does not reverify reporting.

dek.text: San Antonio will repeat its count of loose dogs with a phone on a vehicle window and object detection software. Automated and human review will check the clips, and the survey is a sample.

introduction.text: [Southwest Research Institute is working with the City of San Antonio on an automated survey of unrestrained dogs](c1). [The city's Animal Care Services says it is collaborating with the institute's researchers](c15). [The program pairs machine vision software with cell phone cameras](c2). [A phone mounted to a vehicle window is paired with object detection and data analysis software](c3).

[The automated project will recreate a manual survey from {{number:c9}}](c9), and [it will cover the same {{number:c17}} study areas the city used in that effort](c17). [The city published its own account of the study on {{date:c16}}](c16).

sections.heading: What the software sees and what a person checks

paragraphs.text: [Automated and human review of the video clips will verify that each detected animal was unrestrained](c4). [The same review will record any human supervision, how many dogs were present and whether each dog was owned or a stray](c5).

The release describes the two labels a loose dog can get in terms of how it looks and acts. [Strays appear malnourished and skittish](c6), while [dogs that seem healthier and more approachable are likely owned by local families and are classified as roaming](c7). That is a judgement made from video of a dog on the street, and the record does not yet hold any measure of how often it is right.

[Mike Koets of the institute said the study takes a sampling approach rather than surveying the entire city](c12). [The city says the same thing in its own release. Because the project samples, it is not intended to count every unrestrained dog in San Antonio](c19).

[The Animal Care Services statistics page links to a 2019 Unrestrained Dog Study](c22). Its findings are not part of this account, so no 2019 count appears here, and the comparison the new survey is built to make can't be stated yet.

[Field research is expected to run through December 2026](c20). [The institute will then compile a final report with summary data and videos of the dogs it observed](c11), and [it will forward that report to Animal Care Services](c21). [ACS Director Jon Gary called the study another tool for understanding where unrestrained dogs are being seen](c14). Questions about the results belong with the department, which receives the report.
